task_title: Fast release publication — the undelivered half of GH #449: tag-to-published-artifacts in single-digit minutes via self-hosted release builds started at release-PR merge

Delivered AC1, AC2 and AC4 via PR #573 (merged to main 19:44:40Z as 267b42d7; commits 31a3f64c, e3f10495, 6b279798). AC3 and AC5 are deliberately SPLIT OUT to gate task cas-2ce6 and are NOT claimed here.

AC1 — BASELINE MEASURED. Tag push -> published, from the GitHub API: v3.1.0 13m18s, v3.0.0 14m55s, v3.2.0 20m03s, v2.72.0 26m26s, and v3.4.0 15m33s (933s; the last cold-path release, measured live today with the new receipt tool). Mean 18m03s over five releases. The critical path is the two COLD platform builds in every one of them: on v3.4.0, Build macOS ARM64 was 15m13s and Build Linux x86_64 12m09s of a 15m33s release, while Create Release itself took 17 seconds and Verify Release Inputs (4m54s) ran in parallel. macOS ARM64 is the long pole and there is no Mac in the fleet, so a self-hosted Linux speedup alone provably cannot reach the <10 minute target — building at release-PR merge is the only sufficient lever. That finding is what shaped the whole design.

AC2 — ARCHITECTURE IMPLEMENTED. New .github/workflows/release-prebuild.yml builds both shipped artifacts on the release-PR merge to main, behind a cheap gate (scripts/detect-pending-release.sh: every release-train crate on one semver, a CHANGELOG heading for it, and no such tag on origin). The gate is self-disarming once the tag exists, so ordinary main pushes stay cheap. release.yml gained prebuilt-lookup (scripts/find-release-prebuild.sh), which adopts only a successful prebuild run whose head_sha is exactly the tagged commit with both artifacts present and unexpired; commit identity, not tree identity, matching what check-release-preflight.sh already enforces. On a hit both platform build jobs skip and the tag only downloads, audits and publishes. The lookup is fail-safe — no run, partial run, expired artifact, API outage, unset inputs all decline and fall back to the unchanged cold path, so the accelerator can never be the reason a release cannot ship. Publication is fail-closed on exactly one complete supply path (adopted AND both builds skipped, or no prebuild AND both builds succeeded), with verify required either way, and it re-extracts and re-audits the exact Linux executable it uploads plus records both sha256 digests. The codesign gate (cas-67c1) travels with whichever job produces Darwin bytes: both producing jobs re-sign after strip and run `codesign --verify --verbose=4` before packaging, so nothing downstream can publish unsigned bytes.

FIRST LIVE RECEIPT for the load-sensitive half: the #573 merge push itself triggered Release Prebuild (run 32410322395, headSha 267b42d7, success). The gate job ran 7 seconds, logged `pending=false / reason=v3.4.0 already exists on origin`, and every downstream lane skipped. An ordinary main push therefore costs seven seconds of one ubuntu job and opens nothing — no hosted macOS runner, no self-hosted lane, no compilation. The standing CI-load policy is intact and the self-disarming behaviour is confirmed on real data.

AC4 — TRUST POSTURE UNCHANGED, ROUTING PINNED. Self-hosted routing uses ci.yml's two-key pattern: the label is selected BEFORE runner assignment behind opt-in `vars.CASSY_RELEASE_SELF_HOSTED` (left unset per operator instruction, so every lane currently runs hosted exactly as before), then scripts/check-release-runner-trust.sh re-asserts on the machine itself — push event, canonical repository, routing enabled, ref in {refs/heads/main, refs/tags/v*}, CARGO_TARGET_DIR and SCCACHE_DIR isolated under /var/lib/cassy-actions, sccache port 4227, non-root. The only contents:write job is pinned to ubuntu-latest and the contract forbids the box's label from appearing in it. scripts/test-ci-test-tiers.sh keeps all 596 pre-existing assertions and adds a fast-publication section pinning the trigger surface, the pending-release gate, audit and codesign parity between prebuild and fallback, fail-safe lookup, fail-closed publication, both routing keys, and hosted-only publication. Four new self-tests (42 assertions) are wired into `make -C cas-cli test-ci-tiers` so none can go stale unrun.

AC3 and AC5 — OPEN, tracked by cas-2ce6. A sub-600s receipt on a real release, and closing GH #449 on it, require the next version-bump merge to arm the prebuild and then a tag push; the worker pre-push hook forbids workers from pushing tags, so the demonstration is inherently supervisor/operator work. The tooling for it is delivered and already exercised on a real release: scripts/release-latency-receipt.sh measures from the FIRST Release run of the tag so a rerun cannot flatter the number, and on v3.4.0 it correctly exited non-zero with "took 933s from tag push to publication, over the 600s budget". AC2 — ARCHITECTURE IMPLEMENTED. New .github/workflows/release-prebuild.yml builds both shipped artifacts on the release-PR merge to main, behind a cheap gate (scripts/detect-pending-release.sh: every release-train crate on one semver, a CHANGELOG heading for it, and no such tag on origin). The gate is self-disarming once the tag exists, so ordinary main pushes stay cheap. release.yml gained prebuilt-lookup (scripts/find-release-prebuild.sh), which adopts only a successful prebuild run whose head_sha is exactly the tagged commit with both artifacts present and unexpired; commit identity, not tree identity, matching what check-release-preflight.sh already enforces. On a hit both platform build jobs skip and the tag only downloads, audits and publishes. The lookup is fail-safe — no run, partial run, expired artifact, API outage, unset inputs all decline and fall back to the unchanged cold path, so the accelerator can never be the reason a release cannot ship. Publication is fail-closed on exactly one complete supply path (adopted AND both builds skipped, or no prebuild AND both builds succeeded), with verify required either way, and it re-extracts and re-audits the exact Linux executable it uploads plus records both sha256 digests. The codesign gate (cas-67c1) travels with whichever job produces Darwin bytes: both producing jobs re-sign after strip and run `codesign --verify --verbose=4` before packaging, so nothing downstream can publish unsigned bytes.

FIRST LIVE RECEIPT for the load-sensitive half: the #573 merge push itself triggered Release Prebuild (run 32410322395, headSha 267b42d7, success). The gate job ran 7 seconds, logged `pending=false / reason=v3.4.0 already exists on origin`, and every downstream lane skipped. An ordinary main push therefore costs seven seconds of one ubuntu job and opens nothing — no hosted macOS runner, no self-hosted lane, no compilation. The standing CI-load policy is intact and the self-disarming behaviour is confirmed on real data.

AC4 — TRUST POSTURE UNCHANGED, ROUTING PINNED. Self-hosted routing uses ci.yml's two-key pattern: the label is selected BEFORE runner assignment behind opt-in `vars.CASSY_RELEASE_SELF_HOSTED` (left unset per operator instruction, so every lane currently runs hosted exactly as before), then scripts/check-release-runner-trust.sh re-asserts on the machine itself — push event, canonical repository, routing enabled, ref in {refs/heads/main, refs/tags/v*}, CARGO_TARGET_DIR and SCCACHE_DIR isolated under /var/lib/cassy-actions, sccache port 4227, non-root. The only contents:write job is pinned to ubuntu-latest and the contract forbids the box's label from appearing in it. scripts/test-ci-test-tiers.sh keeps all 596 pre-existing assertions and adds a fast-publication section pinning the trigger surface, the pending-release gate, audit and codesign parity between prebuild and fallback, fail-safe lookup, fail-closed publication, both routing keys, and hosted-only publication. Four new self-tests (42 assertions) are wired into `make -C cas-cli test-ci-tiers` so none can go stale unrun.

AC3 and AC5 — OPEN, tracked by cas-2ce6. A sub-600s receipt on a real release, and closing GH #449 on it, require the next version-bump merge to arm the prebuild and then a tag push; the worker pre-push hook forbids workers from pushing tags, so the demonstration is inherently supervisor/operator work. The tooling for it is delivered and already exercised on a real release: scripts/release-latency-receipt.sh measures from the FIRST Release run of the tag so a rerun cannot flatter the number, and on v3.4.0 it correctly exited non-zero with "took 933s from tag push to publication, over the 600s budget". task_title: Phase 4 fix round (index repair): bounded lock acquisition, repair failures must not disable background indexing, snapshot-after-lock, all-or-nothing legacy-root retirement, bounded maintenance-arm hold
close_reason:
All five Phase 4 findings plus the three supervisor-requested additions are delivered and merged. factory/fast-robin-31 commits b5b71d69 (merged at bc6944d9) and 5a1b144c (merged at c24f43c5); both confirmed ancestors of the epic tip.

PROOF at the epic tip: 524 lib tests pass across legacy_index + daemon + doctor + hybrid_search. retrieval_eval_test 26/26 (unaffected). `cargo clippy -p cas --lib --tests` clean on every touched file.

BOTH P1 TESTS WERE VERIFIED RED BEFORE BEING MADE GREEN, by temporarily restoring the pre-fix code and then restoring mine (`git diff` clean before commit):
- a_held_meta_lock_returns_busy_instead_of_hanging: FAILED at 30.021s with "Timeout" against the blocking META_LOCK — it reproduced the production hang exactly. Now returns Busy in 3.0s.
- a_failing_legacy_repair_still_indexes_pending_entries: FAILED with "indexed 0" against the early return. Now the cycle keeps indexing and reports the failure.

THE FIVE FINDINGS.
P1-A bounded lock acquisition: `acquire_lock(&META_LOCK)` was an unbounded blocking flock (tantivy declares META_LOCK `is_blocking: true`), so a pre-fix `cas serve` holding the legacy root hung `doctor --fix` and, through `run_maintenance`, wedged the whole daemon select! loop. Repair now uses a non-blocking twin of the lock with a 3s deadline and returns a typed `LegacyRepairOutcome::Busy`; doctor renders a Warning naming condition and remedy, the daemon skips the cycle.
P1-B repair failure must not disable indexing: `generate_bm25_index` no longer returns early. Repair errors, Busy skips and unswept-file counts all land in `IndexingResult.errors` and the cycle still drains the pending queue.
P2-A snapshot after the lock: order is now probe-meta -> writer-lock -> snapshot -> requeue -> meta-lock -> retire, pinned by a test asserting a contended repair mutates neither the pending queue nor the legacy root.
P2-B recoverable retirement: ids are durably re-queued first, `meta.json` goes first (after which the root can no longer strand anything), per-file removal failures are tolerated and COLLECTED instead of aborting, and `.managed.json` goes last so a partial run leaves exactly the list the next run resumes from. A `sweep_managed_files` path handles "meta.json gone, .managed.json present".
P2-C bounded per-cycle work: `LegacyRepairLimits { batch_size, max_per_run }`; the daemon passes its configured budget, `doctor --fix` passes `unbounded()`.

THE THREE ADDITIONS.
(1) Residual race closed one level up, at BOTH call sites. tantivy 0.25 exposes no timeout on `IndexReader`'s own META_LOCK acquisition, so the inner probe cannot cover the window between probe and `Index::reader()`. `repair_legacy_index_bounded` runs repair on a dedicated thread and abandons it after a wall-clock budget — 20s daemon, 300s doctor. Detached-thread safety is argued rather than assumed: the worker holds no lock of ours, its re-queue is idempotent, retirement takes the writer lock so it cannot race a later attempt, and doctor exiting mid-sweep is safe because ids are re-queued before any delete and `.managed.json` survives.
(2) Coverage at both sites. `doctor_fix_against_a_held_legacy_lock_warns_within_a_bounded_time` (extracted `legacy_index_autofix` to make `--fix` drivable) and `a_held_legacy_lock_does_not_wedge_the_daemon_cycle` — the latter added in 5a1b144c after I re-read the requirement and found I had tested only one site. Plus two wrapper tests: zero budget -> Busy naming "budget", 60s budget -> the real outcome, so the bound cannot silently swallow every repair.
(3) P3 #7 in count-and-report form. `non_entry_documents` / `retired_non_entry_documents` tally by doc type; doctor warns naming exactly what was dropped, the daemon pushes one error row per type, and `requeued_entries` is documented as counting entry IDS not documents. I did NOT auto-reindex those types: `mark_index_pending_batch` is entries-only, so a real re-queue means reaching into the task/rule/skill/spec stores and calling `reindex_all` — supervisor confirmed that stays out of scope and recorded it on cas-c6c7.

P3 #5 taken because it was three lines: retirement removes the `.tantivy-*.lock` files it created, after dropping its own guards. #6 and #8 filed by the supervisor as cas-c6c7 and cas-a6d6.

TWO SELF-INFLICTED DEADLOCKS I HIT AND FIXED, recorded because the trap is subtle and bit twice:
1. Holding META_LOCK across the snapshot read deadlocks the process against itself — `Index::reader()` acquires META_LOCK internally, which is literally its documented purpose, and the lock is blocking. My first implementation hung three tests. Fixed by probing the meta lock (acquire non-blocking, drop immediately) before opening any reader, and holding it only for the deletion phase.
2. The same trap in my own new doctor test, which asserted on `inspect_legacy_index` while still holding the lock and hung >420s. Fixed by dropping the guard before the assertion.
The rule: anything that opens a tantivy `IndexReader` must not run under META_LOCK. It is in the module docs and in both tests' comments; the supervisor saved it as a durable memory.

AC2 — deletion, not enablement, with the reason and the numbers. Removed `SearchOptions::{boost_feedback, boost_recency, boost_importance, recency_half_life}`, `SearchIndex::apply_boosts` and its call site, the test-only setter and the module doc example. hybrid.rs:547 deliberately untouched per direction.

AC3 — harness gate green on the final configuration, and the committed baseline is UNCHANGED by the deletion. That is the cleanest available proof the removed code was dead: deleting it did not move a single digit.

AC4 — scoped tests pass (22 + 113 above).

THE FINDING. The boosts were not worse; their output was never read. `SearchIndex::search` wrote the boosted value into `score`/`boosted_score` and left `bm25_score` raw; `HybridSearch::search` — the only production consumer — read `r.bm25_score`, discarding it one line later. The boost-induced reordering was discarded too (results are mapped to (id, score) pairs and re-fused), and `truncate(opts.limit)` could have preserved a membership effect but the production caller passes limit = entries*2, so it never bites. No caller of `SearchIndex::search` exists outside `HybridSearch`, and `search_unified` (the `mcp__cas__search` tool) never called apply_boosts at all. Ten arms x three mode combinations produced ONE distinct result per combination.

That the null is real rather than a wiring failure in my experiment is proven by the temporal control: flipping `enable_temporal` through the same options struct changes the BM25 result set (189 -> 185) and its entire head.

PREMISE CORRECTION I RAISED AND THE SUPERVISOR APPROVED: the decision rule named the ambient selectors, but `ambient_recall.rs` never enters `hybrid_search` (verified by grep), so they can neither regress nor improve — applied literally the rule would have mandated deletion regardless of the evidence. Rule re-scoped onto `helpful_memories_production`; ambient reported as measured invariants that demonstrate the scoping.

CORPUS vs CODE INERTNESS, as requested: `feedback` is CORPUS-limited (4/189 entries have helpful_count>0, ZERO have harmful_count, so the multiplier is ~1.0 for 185/189) with the re-open condition tied to cas-8f93's attribution populating at scale plus a larger fixture; `importance` is CODE-limited (158/189 above 0.5, inert purely from the field read); `recency` is neither — inert alone, but it cancels importance's gain when the temporal channel is on. That interaction is only visible because of the paired enable_temporal runs; a single-config A/B would have reported "all boosts do nothing" and hidden it.

COUNTERFACTUAL, measured then reverted (git diff clean): patching hybrid.rs to read `r.score` makes `importance` worth +7.2% P@5 / +6.9% R@5. I did NOT act on it — that is one case out of 56 flipping, inside re-labeling noise, and the change also shifts the BM25 channel from raw ~30-scale to calibrated 0-1 into fusion. Filed as cas-e7ae and referenced by id in the addendum, framed defect-not-dead-feature with the fusion-input caveat.

HARNESS, per direction: the scorer-swap rig is retained and reusable (cas-3b80, the cas-e7ae fusion decision) but carries NO config for deleted code — `ScorerConfig` holds only `temporal`. `ConfigurableHybridScorer` calls the real `contextual_overlap_bonus` (re-exposed `pub(crate)`) rather than copying it, and `the_scorer_replica_matches_production_under_the_production_config` holds it ranking-identical to the real `HybridContextScorer` on all 56 cases in both query modes. No number from an unpinned replica was ever reported.

ONE HONEST ASYMMETRY I SURFACED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED: `enable_temporal` was kept because the channel is real at the search boundary, but its effect does NOT reach the @5 metric on this fixture — build_start's tier filter, the overlap bonus and the high-importance-preference sort dominate the survivors, and the top-5 truncates before the temporal reordering matters. I first wrote a test asserting the arms must differ; it failed, and the honest fix was to assert the equality plus its reason rather than to weaken the claim quietly. So: the boosts were discarded at the field read (never consumed); temporal is consumed but washed out downstream. Different failure modes, and the second is one more reason tier starvation (cas-763b) gates ranking work on the shipped path — on live_tiers no arm moved any metric at all.

task_title: Factory: a Codex worker whose first turn dies with codex_error_info=unauthorized (revoked refresh token) must be reported FAILED at spawn, not left "assigned, not started" for 34 minutes
close_reason:
A worker killed by its harness account is now reported and its task given back, and the spawn that would create one is refused up front. Commit 1916ed70 on factory/mighty-raven-39, merged to main through the protected queue as PR #694; landed main is 94e7de27, and 1916ed70 is confirmed an ancestor of origin/main from this worktree.

Root cause read from the incident's own rollout rather than inferred: in the Codex rollout for 2026-09-03T14-12-58 each of the two turns is an `event_msg` `task_complete` carrying `last_agent_message: null` and an error whose `codex_error_info` is `unauthorized` and whose message is "Your access token could not be refreshed because your refresh token was revoked. Please log out and sign in again.", at 2428ms and 1234ms. Nothing in the factory read that field, so four workers stayed registered with fresh heartbeats, held their tasks, and produced only a soft "ASSIGNED BUT UNSTARTED — possible missed wake" after 300 seconds. The operator found out 34 minutes later.

The fix has two halves because the failure has two moments.

Before the spawn: `preflight_account_auth` runs in factory_spawn_workers immediately before the request becomes worktrees. For each distinct account a request resolves to — the spec's own config_dir, else the captured requester account — it runs the existing bounded probe through the new `capability::probe_account_auth` (`codex login status`, `claude auth status --json`, the same probes `cas factory doctor` uses) and refuses the spawn naming that account directory and the exact re-login command, stating that no worktree was created and no task assigned. Only an affirmative Unavailable refuses: an absent CLI, a probe that timed out, or a harness with no account plumbing is absence of evidence, and a preflight that failed closed on its own unreliability would ground the factory over a slow binary. The whole preflight is bounded at five seconds and each distinct account is probed once. The pre-existing `preflight_codex_config_dir` is untouched and still proves only that an auth.json file exists — which is exactly what a revoked token defeats.

After it: `relay_auth_failed_workers` runs on the same lifecycle tick as the usage-limit relay, scanning at most every fifteen seconds. On evidence of an account failure it releases the worker's task bindings back to open first — the held task is what blocks the epic, and it must not depend on a relay write succeeding — then records the spawn as failed rather than registered in the spawn audit, and relays one message to the supervisor naming the worker, the harness's own words, the remedy for that specific account, and how many tasks were released. Episodes are deduplicated by agent id plus evidence timestamp so the supervisor is told once per failure rather than once per scan, and a failed relay deliberately leaves the dedupe key unset so the next scan retries instead of losing the report.

The scanners live in a new pure module, cas-cli/src/factory_auth_health.rs, over an AuthFailureEvidence of Failed / Healthy / Unavailable, covering Codex rollouts and Claude transcripts. Two policies are deliberate and tested: latest-terminal-turn-wins, so a transient authorization failure the harness itself retried past cannot kill a working worker, which is the false-positive guard the brief asked for; and Unavailable-is-not-Healthy, so an unreadable transcript can never close an open episode.

Fourteen new tests. Nine over the detectors: the unauthorized first turn with its message and timestamp preserved, a healthy first turn, transient-then-recovered, a turn that failed for an unrelated reason, an empty or unparseable tail reading as Unavailable, Claude OAuth expiry closed by a later assistant answer, and Claude prose mentioning an api key or a 401 that must not be mistaken for a broken account. Four over the preflight policy: a logged-out account refuses while naming the directory and `codex login`, the default account is named as ~/.codex when the caller named none, Unknown and Available both pass, and four specs across three distinct accounts cost exactly three probes with a harness lacking account plumbing never probed. One over the seam: a registered Codex agent with a spawn-time CODEX_HOME reads its own rollout as an account failure. Beyond fixtures, the detector was run against the actual incident rollout on this host through a temporary integration test, which reported the failure with the revoked-token message; that test was removed after the run because it depended on a path outside the repository.

Scoped suites pass: factory_auth_health 9, factory_ops 245, ui::factory 734, capability 7, with the supervisor independently measuring 978 tests in the factory scope in this worktree, and `cargo check -p cas --lib` clean.

Two process facts recorded rather than buried. The commit guard refuses to commit from any branch except the exact worker branch, so basing this work on origin/main in a side branch was impossible; factory/mighty-raven-39 was reset to origin/main and force-pushed with lease after verifying with `git branch --contains` that its previous tip was already contained in the epic branch and two other factory branches, so nothing was lost and the branch merged into main carried no epic content. The supervisor accepted that as safe here and ruled that a shared factory branch must not be force-pushed again without asking first; that ruling is stored as a durable preference so it outlives this session.

One limitation is stated plainly rather than papered over: `relay_auth_failed_workers` itself has no direct unit test, because constructing a FactoryDaemon in-process is not supported by the current test seams and its sibling `relay_usage_limited_workers` has none either. Every primitive it composes — evidence, remedy text, task release, spawn audit, relay enqueue — is independently covered, and the wiring is a single call site in the lifecycle tick.

task_title: coordination shutdown_workers rejects a registered worker by name AND by session id ("Worker target(s) not found") while listing that same worker as known
close_reason:
shutdown_workers target resolution fixed; merged into epic cas-2a89 at 594c3b78 (branch tip 97eecd19).

THE REPORTED SYMPTOM: shutdown_workers rejected an idle worker BY NAME and BY SESSION ID with "Worker target(s) not found", while the same error listed that worker among the known workers.

ROOT CAUSE — three different notions of identity in one handler:
1. The `requested_id` selector matched `worker.id == id || worker.name == id` (name OR id), but the `worker_names` selector matched `worker.name == *name` ONLY. A session id passed through worker_names could therefore never match, while the error printed that id as known. That is the by-session-id half.
2. `worker_names` is typed `Option<String>` — a comma-separated string (crates/cas-mcp/src/types/ops_secondary.rs:561) — and `parse_worker_name_filter` split only on commas. The call was made as `worker_names=["quick-dolphin-15"]`, the JSON array shape the parameter's plural name invites, so the literal bracketed text was compared against the bare name and missed. That is the by-name half.
3. The "Known workers" list in the error was built from a third, scope-filtered set, so a single sentence could assert a target was not found while printing it as known.

WHAT IS NOW TRUE
- One identity definition, `worker_answers_to`: name (case-insensitive, whitespace-trimmed), agent id, or cc_session_id. Ids are compared exactly, because case-folding opaque tokens invites false positives. It is used by the id selector, the names selector, the missing-target computation, and both of worker_status's filters — the three of them disagreeing was the defect, so identity now has exactly one definition.
- `parse_worker_name_filter` strips brackets and quotes per element, so the documented comma-separated form and the JSON-array form resolve to the same identifiers. Bounded and explicit; nothing beyond those two shapes is guessed.
- The error no longer lies. A target that is registered but outside this session's shutdown scope is reported as REFUSED with the reason; only a genuinely absent target is reported as NOT FOUND. The message can no longer claim both about one target.
- Resolution does not depend on the worker having an assigned task or being non-idle. The task text raised this as a candidate cause; I checked rather than assumed, ruled it out, and pinned it with a test built on an Idle, no-task worker — the reporter's exact state — resolving by name, by agent id, and via the array form.

TESTS: `-E 'test(/^mcp::/)'` 953 passed; `--test mcp_tools_test` 343 passed (factory_ops:: alone 338). Supervisor's gate on this tip: 953 mcp:: lib tests plus mcp_tools_test and factory_mcp_ops_test 500 — all passed. New coverage: identity by name, agent id and session id including case and surrounding whitespace; the JSON-array and comma forms both resolving; an idle no-task worker resolving three ways; an unknown target still resolving to nothing; and an over-correction guard proving a different worker, a truncated id prefix, an empty string and a near-miss name all still fail to resolve — widening identity matching is exactly the kind of fix that can quietly make a destructive action match too much.

task_title: GH #703 (part 2): worktree_merge reports LOCAL ONLY on a non-fast-forward target push and suggests a git push that cannot succeed
close_reason:
GH #703 "Also observed" (the worktree_merge push path) fixed; merged into the epic as 735b1b58 (branch tip b1697a10).

THE REPORTED SYMPTOM: another supervisor's PR landed, origin/staging moved, worktree_merge merged into the stale local target, the push was rejected non-fast-forward, and the receipt announced "origin/staging ... is BEHIND" with "REQUIRED NEXT STEP: git push origin staging" — the inverse of the real condition, followed by the one command that could not succeed.

TWO DEFECTS, BOTH FIXED

1. No pre-merge reconciliation. worktree_merge merged without ever fetching origin/<target>, so once the remote had advanced the push could only be rejected. New `GitOperations::reconcile_target_with_origin` fetches first and classifies the result: AlreadyCurrent, FastForwarded, Diverged, FetchFailed, NoRemote. The handler calls it BEFORE the merge.
   - Strictly behind with no local-only commits: fast-forwarded automatically, with the receipt naming old tip -> new tip and the commit count (supervisor-directed: a fast-forward loses nothing and asking first would add a round trip to every merge).
   - Diverged: refused BEFORE any merge, naming both tips and both ahead/behind counts, with a fetch/merge/retry remedy and an explicit never-force-push line. Refusing after the merge would leave an unpublishable merge commit on the operator's local target to unpick.
   - Fetch failure (offline, auth, unreachable): never blocks. The merge proceeds against the local target and the receipt says so explicitly, warning the push may still be rejected.
   The ahead/behind comparison runs strictly AFTER the fetch, against freshly re-resolved refs; comparing beforehand would judge divergence against a stale tracking ref and could call a clean fast-forward a divergence, or miss a real one. How the fast-forward is applied depends on where the branch is checked out — `git merge --ff-only origin/<target>` in place, otherwise a compare-and-swap `update-ref` passing the old value so a concurrent move loses rather than clobbers — mirroring the existing merge venue split, because a bare update-ref against a checked-out branch would leave that working tree behind its own branch ref.

2. The rejection was classified as a generic failure and rendered with a hard-coded falsehood. `classify_push_rejection` collapsed every non-GH013 failure into one outcome, so the renderer could not distinguish "the remote moved" from "the network died", and the "is BEHIND" claim was baked into the format string rather than derived from the tips. It now has a `NonFastForward` arm matched on git's own stable markers, and the receipt names both tips, says origin is AHEAD, states plainly that a bare push cannot succeed until the two are reconciled, gives the fetch-and-merge remedy, and rules out force-pushing a shared target.

Nothing in this change force-pushes anything.

task_title: GH #698: symbol index fails UTF-16 (BOM) source files with "stream did not contain valid UTF-8" forever — decode BOM-marked UTF-16/UTF-8-BOM files or skip them with a named reason instead of counting a permanent failure
close_reason:
GH #698 fixed; merged into the epic as 4f6ef15e (branch tip 11e573cc).

WHY THE WARNING COULD NEVER CLEAR: the indexer read every candidate with `fs::read_to_string` (cas-cli/src/daemon/indexing.rs), so a UTF-16 file failed with "stream did not contain valid UTF-8" and landed in the scan's error list. `failed_files` is derived as `eligible - indexed`, so that file stayed in the denominator permanently, and `cas index code` — the remediation the doctor line itself printed — re-read the same bytes and failed identically. The remedy was structurally incapable of working, which is why the reporter saw the same three files on Aug 31 and again on Sep 3.

WHAT IS NOW TRUE
- BOM-marked source files are decoded rather than failed: UTF-16 LE, UTF-16 BE, and UTF-8-with-BOM, in a new `daemon::source_text` module using std only. No new dependency was taken for three byte patterns.
- Decoding is strict, never lossy. An odd byte count after a UTF-16 BOM (truncated) and an unpaired surrogate (malformed) each produce a distinct named skip rather than U+FFFD replacement text indexed as if it were the author's code. Silent bad data in a symbol index outlives a loud error.
- A file that genuinely cannot be decoded is SKIPPED WITH A REASON and leaves the eligible denominator, so coverage reaches 100% of eligible instead of parking at 2,350/2,355. Skips are persisted separately from failed_files (migration 254, with the existing scan row preserved and defaulting to zero skips until the next scan reclassifies it), so a rerun cannot resurrect a warning no retry could clear.
- Doctor names the skipped files and attaches NO remediation to them, in both the warning and the healthy line. Printing "run `cas index code`" beside a file that can never be indexed is what trains operators to ignore doctor.

SECOND DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED, which the issue did not report and nobody had noticed: `read_to_string` ACCEPTED UTF-8-with-BOM, because a BOM is valid UTF-8. The BOM therefore reached the parser glued to the first token and the file indexed "successfully" with a subtly wrong first symbol. It produced bad data quietly instead of failing loudly, which is exactly why it went unreported. The BOM is now stripped, pinned by a test asserting the first symbol is findable by its real name.

task_title: Client half of revision-based conflict resolution (gated on petra-stella-cloud#41)
close_reason:
Client half of revision-based conflict resolution delivered; merged into the epic as 037a6300 (branch tip 642c1803).

WHAT IS NOW TRUE
- Server revisions decide sync conflicts; clocks decide only when revisions cannot. When both sides carry a revision and they differ, the higher wins and the timestamps are not consulted at all — that is what stops a machine with a wrong clock from silently winning or losing. Equal revisions, or either side missing one, fall through to the original timestamp comparison unchanged.
- Revision comparison arbitrates the KeepRecent strategy only. An explicit RemoteWins/LocalWins is an operator choice and stays authoritative (supervisor confirmed this is correct as shipped).
- `sync_revisions` ledger (migration 251) stores the last observed server revision per (entity_type, entity_id), monotonic on write so a replayed older envelope cannot roll a row backwards — that value becomes the base revision of the next push, and a rolled-back base would be rejected forever.
- Pull records each applied row's revision only AFTER the row is written, for entries, tasks, rules and skills, on both the personal and team paths. The ledger never claims a revision whose body this machine has not seen.
- Push declares the base revision as a decimal string when the ledger knows one and OMITS the key when it does not (omission selects the server's timestamp-LWW compatibility path). Any body-embedded revision is stripped first. Nothing is ever synthesized: the server drops a row whose revision it cannot parse, and a fabricated "0" against an existing row is a guaranteed conflict.
- Push receipts are consumed: the echoed new revision is read from the per-type accepted map (personal at top level, team nested under `synced`), so the next push declares an acceptable base without a re-pull. A revision_conflict is treated as retryable rather than parked — a lost race is a stale base, not a bad row — and the proven-stale base is FORGOTTEN rather than replaced with the server's current_revision, because adopting a revision whose body we never looked at would let the next push silently overwrite someone else's change.
- Conflict journal rows carry both revisions (migration 252, nullable), threaded through the single journal_local_overwrite funnel; strategy_label() distinguishes a "revision" decision from "timestamp_lww" so an audit can tell the two regimes apart.
- SyncQueue repairs its own sync_conflicts columns on init rather than depending on migration order: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cannot widen an existing table, so a store created before this change would otherwise fail every conflict insert until migration 252 happened to run. The queue owns those writes.

THE AUDIT THAT MADE IT REAL: wiring the resolver was not enough. upsert_task (the PERSONAL task pull) and upsert_skill compared updated_at INLINE and never called resolve_conflict, so the comparison was unit-tested and would almost never have run against a real sync. Both now go through remote_supersedes_local. Because the revision arrives on the raw wire row while the decision happens inside typed upsert helpers, the pull stages incoming revisions on the syncer (cleared at pull start) instead of threading an argument through six signatures where one missed site would silently revert that entity kind to clock comparison.

CONTRACT VERIFIED LIVE AND READ-ONLY, BEFORE CODING AND AGAIN BEFORE CLAIMING RULES/SKILLS: revision is present on 100% of pulled rows (personal tasks 114/114, entries 1019/1019, dependencies 3533/3533; team 111/111, 79/79, 4401/4401) and is a decimal STRING — a lexicographic compare ranks "9" above "10" and would invert every conflict from a row's tenth edit onward, which a dedicated test pins. Rules and skills genuinely carry revisions too (personal rules 2/2; team rules 22/22, skills 3/3), so recording them is contract-backed rather than synthesized. Push-side contract read from the deployed cloud source: the field is plain revision per entity object, omission selects legacy, a malformed value drops the row as invalid_revision, and reason is treated as an open string.

TESTS (scoped filtersets — a plain substring filter runs zero tests under the guard): test(/^cloud::/) 325 passed, test(/^cli::cloud::/) 81 passed, test(/^migration::/) 150 passed; combined filterset 556. Supervisor's gate on this tip: 1148 lib tests across cloud::, cli::cloud::, migration::, store::, cli::doctor::, mcp::tools::core::task plus mcp_tools_test and cli_test integration, all passed. The acceptance evidence is a real pull, not the unit API: a full team pull where the cloud row is an hour newer by the clock but one revision behind, and the local row survives; it failed before commit 642c1803. Clock skew is covered in both directions, plus a backward-compatibility matrix over all three revision-absence combinations against newer-remote, newer-local and identical timestamps.

Commits: caf73435 (comparison, ledger, journal), 315efac8 (base revision on push, receipts, revision_conflict), 9c9090d9 (epic merge, m250 collision renumber to m251/m252, migration::tests cursor pin and its three pending vectors moved to 252), 642c1803 (make the comparison fire on real pulls).

OPERATOR NOTE FOR THE RELEASE: the default team strategy is RemoteWins, so on a default-configured team pull the revision comparison does not fire — RemoteWins already answers the question. Revisions arbitrate KeepRecent: personal pulls, and teams configured for "keep whichever is newer".

task_title: verification add fails fast with "database is locked" under store contention while coordination message writes in the same seconds succeed — add busy_timeout/retry parity across write paths
close_reason:
Root cause: not a missing busy_timeout. The verification add handler already set the 5s SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT (verification_tools.rs:466); the defect was conn.unchecked_transaction() at :473, which is DEFERRED. The block reads the dispatch and the verifier capability before it inserts, so it held a read snapshot and had to UPGRADE to a writer — and SQLite answers that upgrade with SQLITE_BUSY without ever invoking the busy handler, because blocking there could deadlock two readers upgrading at once. The configured timeout was therefore silently irrelevant and the call failed in milliseconds, which is exactly why four consecutive verification writes failed while single-statement message and notes writes in the same seconds succeeded: their busy handler does apply.

Reproduced twice before any fix. Outside CAS with sqlite3 at .timeout 5000: BEGIN; SELECT; (foreign commit); INSERT fails immediately, while BEGIN IMMEDIATE; SELECT; INSERT succeeds. In-code as a permanent regression test: a_deferred_read_then_write_fails_instantly_despite_the_busy_timeout asserts the failure arrives in under 500ms with a 5s timeout configured.

Delivered:
1. shared_db::begin_immediate_with_retry acquires BEGIN IMMEDIATE — where the busy handler applies — with the same jittered backoff as with_write_retry. The retry envelope is strictly narrower than the transactional block: retries occur only while acquiring the lock, and once the transaction is open the body runs exactly once, so the single-use verifier capability the body consumes cannot be double-consumed. The verification add handler uses it.
2. cas-cli/src/memory_migration/reindex.rs read every knowledge page body from disk inside its write transaction, holding the store's write lock across N filesystem reads. Bodies are now read first; the transaction contains only database work.
3. Sibling audit: three sites inspected and deliberately left unchanged because each writes first and therefore takes the lock where the busy handler applies — purge_fixtures.rs:233, recording_store/store_impl.rs:512, event_store.rs:321.
4. journal_size_limit = 64 MiB on connection open, pinned by a test, so a long-lived writer fleet stops leaving a 389 MB WAL behind for 1,137 live frames. TRUNCATE-on-quiet was deliberately excluded per supervisor ruling: a checkpoint policy can stall a writer and belongs in its own task.
5. The give-up error states the wait attempted — "database busy for 5.3s across 6 attempt(s); another connection held the write lock for the whole wait" — instead of the bare sqlite text that made the original report un-triageable.

Fix (241e8095 + amendment fc72a22b on factory/eager-owl-7):
- `SqliteCodeVectorStore::reconcile(force)` — drops queue rows with no eligible symbol, re-arms failed rows (all on force; otherwise all but a documented permanent-input deny-list, `is_retryable_vector_failure`), rewrites rows whose content_hash drifted from the symbol (the drain refuses those forever, cloud/code_embeddings.rs:106-110, so they were permanent pending), and enqueues eligible symbols with no row. - `daemon::indexing::reconcile_code_vector_queue()` runs at the end of `reconcile_code_tree` (daemon startup + default `cas index code`) and from index_cmd for path-scoped runs; it also deletes the LMDB vectors of dropped rows. Counts print as a line and as a JSON object.
- Contention, three layers: the vector-queue writes (`retire`, `sync_file_symbols`, schema DDL on open) take the write lock up front with bounded retry; the code-store writes on the retire/publish path (`add_file`, `add_symbol`, `delete_symbol`, `delete_symbols_in_file`, `delete_file`) go through `shared_db::with_write_retry`, and the two batch writers through `with_immediate_write_txn`; the BM25 publish waits out a writer lock held by a concurrent `cas serve` with one WriterLockBudget shared across the run (per-file retries would have multiplied across 592 files).

task_title: `cas integrate mecha-cassy` rewrites only the user-level allowlist; a project-local `.cas/proxy.toml` with the retired slack_* names shadows it, so doctor keeps warning and its remediation line is false
close_reason:
`cas integrate mecha-cassy` now resolves and repairs the project `.cas/proxy.toml` that shadows the machine registration, so doctor's remediation line clears the warning it prints. Merged into the epic as 2af34a4c (commits 1bfdab8d + 7e7ca945).

Root cause, verified at file:line rather than assumed: crates/cas-mcp-proxy/src/config.rs:328 `merged.allowlist = project.allowlist` — a project proxy file REPLACES the machine allowlist rather than widening it — combined with `run()` only ever loading and saving `paths.user_proxy`. The retired slack_* routes therefore stayed authoritative through any number of re-runs while the command reported "already-configured" and exited 2.

Fix, one production file (cas-cli/src/cli/integrate/mecha_cassy.rs; the proxy crate is untouched):
- `run()` takes `project_proxy: Option<&Path>`; `execute()` resolves it via the same `find_cas_root` ancestor walk the proxy loader uses, so the command repairs the very file doctor reads.
- The file is edited with `toml_edit`, not round-tripped through `ProxyConfig`: comments, key order, multi-line array shape and every unrelated server and route survive byte-for-byte.
- Its mecha-cassy routes are rewritten to MECHA_CASSY_TOOLS. Its `[servers.mecha-cassy]` block is removed only when it parses equal to the machine registration this run wrote or found current; a block that differs is an override, such as a project aimed at a staging hub, and is kept and named, because dropping it would silently move that project to another endpoint. Keeping is not a change, so a run over an override stays idempotent.
- `report.allowlist` is now the effective policy, so drift is measured against what will actually dispatch, and "already-configured" cannot be printed while a shadowing file drifts.
- A project file that names no hub route is left untouched and reported with the exact routes to add, rather than offered a re-run that cannot work.
- `ToolDrift::describe` takes the source path, so the doctor drift row names the file the stale entries live in.

Live-hub verification with the built binary, both branches. Durable evidence: /home/pippenz/.cas/artifacts/cas-a0ab/demo.txt with proxy.toml.{before,after} and override.proxy.toml.{before,after}. (A) A project file carrying the reported 6-entry allowlist plus a duplicate server block went from `warning | hub tool contract drifted … allowlist in <project>/.cas/proxy.toml: [mecha_post, mecha_read, slack_list_channels, slack_post_message, slack_read_channel, slack_upload_file]` to `ok | registered …; hub answered with 2 tool(s): mecha_read, mecha_post` after ONE run, exit 0, with the file's comment preserved and the machine registration untouched ("already current"). task_title: Foreign-row peer scan treats every known_repos row as a project and WARNs on test scratch roots ("fresh-proxy … no such table: tasks"); registry must skip artifacts/scratch roots and `cas known-repos` needs a `forget <path>` verb

(1) Registry writes skip disposable roots. `store/known_repos.rs` gains `RegistrySkip{Artifacts,Scratch,Temp}` + `registry_skip()`; `register_repo`, `register_repo_strict` and `worktree::discovery::seed` all consult it and log the reason at debug. A skip returns Ok, not Err, so the boot paths that `?` the strict call keep booting. Artifacts roots resolve from three sources — the default host artifacts directory, the candidate's own `.cas/config.toml` (an artifacts copy carries the config it was copied from), and the ambient project store — so a configured `[factory] artifacts_root` is honoured. The temp rule is narrow on purpose: only a directory directly under the system temp directory carrying a `temp_hygiene::TEMP_ROOT_PREFIXES` name. A blanket system-temp rule was tried and rejected, because every TestEnvGuard fixture HOME is itself a system-temp directory; that rule would have silently disabled registration across the suite and for any operator whose checkout lives on a temp mount.

(2) Peer enumeration separates "not a project store" from "unreadable". `read_snapshot` split into `open_read_only` + `snapshot_from_conn`; new `read_peer_snapshot` returns `Ok(None)` when the peer DB has no `tasks` table. Bindings are removed here unlike `prune-missing`, which preserves them on purpose — forget is an explicit operator instruction about that exact repository, so a selector left aimed at it would resolve to a root the registry no longer knows. task_title: cas update --all-projects silently skips local projects that are not in known_repos and never migrates the user-level ~/.cas store — 18 projects at schema 236 and ~/.cas at 248 after "N projects refreshed · 0 failed"
close_reason:
Root cause was not the brief's "discovery only enumerates known_repos" — the filesystem scan was structurally dead on every real host. cas-cli/src/cli/update.rs scan_for_projects did `if root.join(".cas").is_dir() { insert; return; }`; every host that has run Cassy has ~/.cas, so scanning $HOME inserted $HOME and returned on the first call, and discover_local_projects then removed $HOME as host state. Net: zero filesystem discovery, ever, so discovery collapsed to the 139 known_repos rows — only ~11 of which are live Petrastella projects, the rest dead /tmp dirs. That is exactly the "16-17 projects refreshed" number. The same early return also hid every project nested under a parent project, and ~/Petrastella/.cas exists, so even a working walk would have stopped at Petrastella and never reached pixel-hive. Measured: 29 dirs under ~/Petrastella have .cas/cas.db vs 11 registered.

FIXED (all in update.rs; four asks all landed):
(1) Registration — serve (mcp/server/runtime.rs:119), the factory daemon (cli/factory/daemon.rs:35) and init already upsert, so update was the gap: every scan-discovered project the sweep refreshes is now register_repo()'d, so discovery converges with no manual step. Added `cas update --register <path>` (ensure_host_schema + register_repo_strict; refuses a dir with no .cas) for projects outside $HOME/CAS_PROJECT_ROOTS or deeper than the bound.
(2) Discovery — both halves of the either/or, split by whether there is anything to migrate. scan_for_projects records a project and keeps descending (MAX_SCAN_DEPTH=8), never entering a .cas/ — load-bearing, since .cas/worktrees/<lane> and .cas/backup/<stamp> both contain a cas.db and are not projects — nor hidden/vendored dirs. discover_local_projects returns ProjectDiscovery{projects, unregistered, skipped_unregistered}: scan-only dirs with a cas.db are refreshed and registered; a .cas with no cas.db is listed as "not refreshed (unregistered): N — run `cas update` inside them or `cas update --register <path>`" and counted in the banner.
(3) User-level store — refresh_user_level_store() runs migrations + builtins against ~/.cas, printed as its own "[OK] user-level store:" line and carried in JSON as user_level_store{store,status}; never counted in project totals.
(4) Store path — schema_status_json() prefixes all four receipt shapes with "store"; human mode appends the path to "Schema up to date (vN) — <path>" and "Schema updated to vN — <path>". Receipt also gains per-project store + registered.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA MET. Live on this host: dry run went 16-17 -> 43 projects, with pixel-hive, tracetix, verified-path and petra_stella_tools/{aws,logging,project-management,time-tracking} all present; the user-level store is named in both the human line and the JSON receipt; no worktree/backup false positives; 1.2s depth-8 scan of $HOME. Ask (4) paid off immediately — my first attempt inherited CAS_ROOT and silently migrated cas-src instead, and the new "store" field made that visible where the pre-fix line could not distinguish it. That is the operator's exact "says applied but didn't" shape, now impossible to emit.

Supervisor gate on this tip: cli::update + store:: 117 passed, update_all_projects_test + cli_test 53 passed; combined epic tip 348 lib / 100 integration green, cargo check clean.

Verdict ver-e4699a3c3175 pass on vdispatch-44b70827fb6733aca9f75e23cf872ee0. Root-cause correction accepted and recorded by the supervisor. task_title: Release-gate archive-mode fails under load when a child `cas init` hits its 300s watchdog; the gate should raise or disable that budget for its own children
close_reason:
The `cas init` watchdog budget is now settable (CAS_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS, clamped to 3600s), and scripts/release-gate.sh exports 900s for its own children — the gate is itself the slow-CI environment the abort message names. Ordinary `cas init` keeps its 300s; a meaningless override (empty, non-numeric, zero, negative) falls back to the default instead of disabling the watchdog; an over-large one clamps rather than becoming a second opt-out; CAS_INIT_NO_TIMEOUT=1 still disables outright.

The finding that shaped the fix: no gate row runs `cas init` directly. The children that hit 300s live inside integration tests (cas-cli/tests/support/mod.rs:73 runs `init --yes` for every CasSandbox), so a bare export in the gate would have been a no-op — cas-cli/tests/support/mod.rs:106 and cas-cli/src/test_env_guard.rs each scrub every ambient CAS_* variable from their children. Both now carry this one variable across, and only this one: it is a clock, not an identity, and cannot repoint a store or root. Neighbouring names (CAS_INIT_TIMEOUT, CAS_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS_EXTRA, CAS_INIT_NO_TIMEOUT, CAS_INIT_ROOT) are asserted to stay scrubbed, cas-cli/src/lib.rs's process-wide "nothing CAS_* survives" assertion holds against the single stated exemption, and the sandbox test seeds hostile CAS_ROOT/CAS_DIR to prove pinning is untouched.

Backstop: 900s sits above nextest's own per-test kill (slow-timeout 60s x terminate-after 10 = 600s), so inside any suite row nextest still kills and names a genuinely hung test — the raised budget only stops a load-slowed init from failing the row first. Outside a suite row the 3600s ceiling bounds it.

Reproduction command and before/after, contention confined to one core so the rest of the fleet was untouched (isolated HOME/CAS_ROOT under /var/tmp, CAS_TEST_PROTECTED_DBS armed at the real ~/.cas/cas.db, scratch removed):
  for i in 1..6: taskset -c 3 bash -c 'while :; do :; done' &
  taskset -c 3 env CAS_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS=1   target/debug/cas init --yes  -> aborted at 1.07s, exit 3, "cas init: aborting after 1s timeout ... Set CAS_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS=<seconds> to raise this budget on a slow or loaded machine, or CAS_INIT_NO_TIMEOUT=1 to disable the watchdog"
  taskset -c 3 env CAS_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS=900 target/debug/cas init --yes  -> completed in 1.69s, exit 0

task_title: Supervisor panes never wake for ordinary traffic: cas-dab2 gate denies every non-lifecycle row, so worker plans/merge requests/dispatch handoffs are delivered but invisible until the supervisor polls
close_reason:
Supervisor pane wakes are now decided from the sender CAS recorded at enqueue time, and a registered worker's merge request wakes an idle supervisor without a poll.

Delivered on factory/bold-heron-25 tip a3e81f6d, merged to epic/epic-v3-15-5-coordination-follow-ups-duplicate-mes-cas-55aa at c01ce1fa. Four commits: ee4d0dd2 (cherry-pick of true-panther-6's 7f178c0c — verified identical by patch-id, so that branch retires with nothing lost), 07f6361f, ffbc7080, fda51375. Each commit green and each leaves wakes functional; the schema/population half landed before the gate half deliberately, because NULL never wakes and a gate-first landing would have silently killed every wake CAS has today.

WHAT WAS WRONG
1. The reported bug: every non-lifecycle supervisor-addressed row was inbox-only, so the messages whose purpose is to unblock the supervisor waited for a poll (merge request 24346 parked a task in AwaitingMerge; dispatch handoff 24370 blocked a close; an execution plan sat unread while the supervisor sent a status check asking why no plan had arrived).
2. The cas-15f2 bypass, folded in by supervisor ruling 24559: the peer-supervisor allowance sat IN FRONT of cas-3dcb's envelope check and turned on names_a_registered_supervisor(agents, source) — a roster lookup of a caller-settable name. `cas factory message --from "<a real supervisor's name>"` therefore skipped envelope corroboration entirely and obtained a PTY write with arbitrary text. The old unit test modelled the forgery as "the roster said no" and could not see it.

WHAT LANDED
- prompt_queue.origin_agent_id / origin_kind: additive, nullable, written ONLY by CAS's own enqueue path from an already-authenticated caller. QueueOrigin {RegisteredAgent{agent_id}, Daemon, Unattributed}; the agent id is the registry id, not a display name, so role resolution cannot be spoofed by naming someone. No backfill — inventing provenance for rows whose sender was never recorded is the fiction the columns exist to prevent.
- Stamped: MCP coordination message/interrupt and factory clear_context -> RegisteredAgent, taken from the session's registry row and never from display_name, row_source, or get_agent_id()'s literal "unknown" fallback; 11 daemon relay sites -> Daemon. `cas factory message` and bridge POST /message cannot stamp AT ALL — they reach the store through methods that take no origin parameter, so there is no expression in those routes that can produce one. That is enforcement by type system, not a runtime default. Commander/hub is left unstamped deliberately: it has a real authenticated principal, but a device credential is not a registry id and minting one would be the same fiction.
- Gate re-keyed: supervisor_wake_class(sender, supervisor_name, source, prompt). Daemon + a lifecycle/worker-died/spawn/CI/attention envelope; Registered{Supervisor} + not this pane's own echo; Registered{Worker} + a CAS-attached <cas-merge-request>. Unstamped, Unattributed and Unresolvable never wake, whatever the payload says.
- message_status separates wake_not_applicable from wake_declined_by_policy with the reason. One prefix used to cover both a routine chat row and an eligible unblock request the pane refused — opposite facts, and the second hid in a wall of the first.
- Fail-safe: one Daemon-stamped <worker-attention kind="supervisor_unread"> per distinct backlog head, naming the unread count and the oldest sender, emitted from the delivery-stalled scan that previously bounced only to senders. This is how a blocker and a verification handoff reach an idle supervisor, satisfying the acceptance criteria's "or is surfaced by an equivalent unread mechanism" clause.
- Two doc comments corrected where they asserted a property that does not hold (factory_supervisor_overlap::names_a_registered_supervisor, and the gate's copy of the same claim). Both are now marked NOT AN AUTHENTICATION CHECK and retained as display/consistency only.

EVERY ACCEPTANCE CRITERION IS MET
- "A merge request … sent by a registered worker to its supervisor wakes the supervisor pane": met by the Registered{Worker} + <cas-merge-request> class.
- "verification handoff, or blocker … or is surfaced by an equivalent unread mechanism": met by the supervisor_unread backlog relay.
- "a message whose `source` string is caller-set and whose sender is not a registered agent still cannot obtain a PTY write": met, and enforced by the type system at the enqueue side as well as by the gate refusing Unstamped/Unattributed/Unresolvable.
- "message_status distinguishes 'wake not applicable' from 'wake declined by policy' with the reason": met by WakeOutcome, persisted as "wake_not_applicable: <reason>" / "wake_declined_by_policy: <reason>".
- "Duplicate delivery is either fixed or explained with the two writers named": explained and fixed. cas-cdf9 measured ONE writer performing two writes — delivery.rs:855 deliver_to_worker (the teams-inbox write, which Claude Code renders as <teammate-message>) and delivery.rs:876 pty_nudge (the same text typed into the pane, appearing as the bare "CAS provenance:" turn). director_events and surface_unseen_for_recipient are both exonerated by receipt evidence. Fixed at b3d834bb, already in this branch's base. I confirmed the two call sites exist as described; I did not re-derive the store measurements.

THE THREE JUDGEMENT CALLS, all ruled ACCEPTED AS DELIVERED by the supervisor (msg 24587)
1. `source` is still READ, but only for the Daemon class, where CAS wrote both the stamp and the source. Caught against an existing test: a Closed-transition lifecycle row carries a real envelope but no `lifecycle-wake:` prefix, so envelope-only would have started waking supervisors for progress FYIs — the exact cas-dab2 noise. It is authority nowhere.
2. Only the CAS-framed merge request wakes. Blockers and verification handoffs are free text, and waking on them means waking on a keyword — the check class this task removed. They are delivered through the unread-backlog relay above. The supervisor took the separate follow-up for CAS-emitted blocker/verification-dispatch envelopes as his own and instructed me not to open it; that is a future enhancement, not residual work from this task.
3. The peer-supervisor class trusts the stamped registry Supervisor role with no envelope requirement, stated out loud in the code rather than left implicit. There is no supervisor-to-supervisor envelope to corroborate against, and requiring one would kill the wake v3.15.4 just shipped.

Also load-bearing, and easy to misread as tidiness: wake-eligible rows are excluded from the unread count, because the summary is itself a lifecycle-wake row and would otherwise become its own backlog head without end. And `supervisor_unread` is registered in BOTH worker-attention parsers — the wake-corroboration check and message_ack's outbox-key bridge — since missing the second acks the durable notification and leaves the prompt relay visible in every later worker_status.

CLAIM DISCIPLINE, verbatim per ruling 24559: this raises the bar from "the caller must know a prefix and a tag grammar" to "the caller must be an authenticated registered agent". It does NOT defend against a local process with write access to .cas/cas.db, which can insert a row with any origin it likes. Local store write access remains the trust boundary. No stronger claim is made.

TESTS, mine at branch tip a3e81f6d: 1550 passed (cas --lib, filter coordination|message|factory|wake|supervisor), 655 passed (cas-store --lib, whole crate), 165 passed (cas --test factory_mcp_ops_test, whole target), plus scoped 250 / 36 / 3 (ui::factory::daemon::runtime, prompt_revalidation, supervisor_queue). cargo check -p cas --lib --tests and -p cas-store --lib --tests clean.
Supervisor's independent re-run on the merged tree c01ce1fa: cargo check clean; 345/345 lib; 143/143 cas-store prompt_queue; 19/19 factory_mcp_ops_test wake/supervisor/peer.
The cas-15f2 acceptance test now drives the real resolution end to end — it asserts the row from a live MCP supervisor send carries a stamped RegisteredAgent origin, resolves that id in the registry, and feeds the result to the real gate. That is the check cas-15f2 lacked: its flag was passed in by hand and stayed green the entire time production could never resolve it to true. Its forgery case is now the actual attack, a genuinely registered supervisor's name on an unstamped row, instead of a roster miss.

- `report.allowlist` is now the effective policy, so drift is measured against what will actually dispatch, and "already-configured" cannot be printed while a shadowing file drifts.
- A project file that names no hub route is left untouched and reported with the exact routes to add, rather than offered a re-run that cannot work.

The matcher signature now takes artifacts_root, resolved at the call site by new close_reason_artifacts_root(&self.cas_root) (Config::load + resolved_factory_artifacts_root, best effort). task_title: Flaky under load: hub_clean_home_test::concurrent_start_and_restart_leave_exactly_one_lock_owner failed once in the v3.15.1 release gate's full nextest run, passes 3/3 in isolation
close_reason:
Delivered on factory/true-panther-6, frozen at a544276a96e28a952f08b1d2f0acb9389ccd8000; merged by the supervisor into epic cas-cfd3, tip 420ee07d. Verified ver-3bb02e67a9d9 (pass) on vdispatch-ba3604c3c4f6433f0b13b021d2b685d4.

Durable evidence: /home/pippenz/.cas/artifacts/cas-bf90/ (README.md, after-24-iterations.txt, and the four harness scripts). Reproduction command: /home/pippenz/.cas/artifacts/cas-bf90/measure.sh 24 8 — runs `hub start --port 0 --tailscale-serve` and `hub restart --port 0 --tailscale-serve` concurrently against one private HOME under 8 CPU spinners, tallying failures per command, both-fail, and lock-wait timeouts. The recorded receipt was produced by that durable copy.

ROOT CAUSE. Not a timeout being too small. Concurrent `hub start` and `hub restart` both stop the old hub and both try to launch a replacement; whichever arrives second waits on the machine lock, which the winner's brand-new healthy hub legitimately holds for its whole life. Every waiter asked "is the lock FREE?" when the caller cares about "is a satisfying hub LIVE?" — an unsatisfiable condition, not a slow one, which is why no budget increase could have fixed it.

FIX. RelaunchIntent makes the caller's purpose explicit on the shared stop path. stop_with_output takes Option<RelaunchIntent>: Some(..) lets the wait resolve on observing a live hub satisfying those flags; None (plain `hub stop`) is byte-for-byte unchanged, because for stop a live hub is the opposite of success. StopOutcome::AlreadySatisfied forces callers to return rather than fall through — load-bearing twice: the teardown after the wait (remove_process_record, cgroup kill, Tailscale disable) would otherwise dismantle a healthy hub the command does not own, and falling through would recurse stop -> start -> Restart -> stop forever, since with `--port 0` decide_live_start always chooses Restart. The wait never accepts the hub being replaced as its own replacement. Wired into all three stop-to-relaunch callers: the `hub restart` arm, the flags-differ branch of `hub start`, and restart_stale_hub for `cas update`. The launch waiter got the same treatment via running_hub_satisfies_request + wait_for_lock_or_satisfying_hub.

BEFORE / AFTER, same harness, concurrent start+restart under load:
- Before: the losing command failed in ~80% of iterations, ALWAYS after burning the full 10s HUB_LIFECYCLE_TIMEOUT.
- After: 24 iterations, any_fail=0, start_fail=0, restart_fail=0, both_fail=0, lock_wait_timeouts=0; every iteration 150-320ms.
- The integration test itself: failing at 10.18s -> passing at 1.426s.

PER-SITE ATTRIBUTION. Mid-fix, with only the launch waiter done, every residual failure was attributable by message provenance: 5x wait_for_process_and_lock_release, 5x the record-absent bare wait_for_instance_lock, 0x the new launch waiter. Giving the new waiter distinct wording is what made that measurable; three sites previously emitted identical text.

WHERE THE LAST BUG HID. After wiring intent into the `start` flags-differ branch and restart_stale_hub, the test still failed: the `hub restart` arm was `stop(cli)?` + `start(...)`, so it went through the plain stop wrapper and carried no intent. The strengthened assertion caught that deterministically on the first run. The old assertion was `any(success)`, which passed whenever either command happened to win and so hid a ~80% loser-failure rate entirely; without changing it this fix would have shipped looking correct.

SCOPE. serve_foreground's fail-fast acquire_instance_lock unchanged; terminate_failed_launch untouched; no timeout constant changed. wait_for_process_and_lock_release removed as dead code, its quiescence rule and exact error text preserved in wait_for_stop_or_satisfying_hub.

TESTS. hub_clean_home_test 8/8 (was 7/8 with the concurrent test red), lib hub:: 129, lib cli::hub 33, lib cli::update 31. Six new unit tests on running_hub_satisfies_request, and a new integration test proving plain `hub stop` still fails and names why while a hub holds the lock past the deadline. Supervisor's independent gate on the delivered tip: hub::/cli::hub lib 94, hub_clean_home_test 8/8, and 8/8 again on the merged tree.

BOTH-FAIL, stated plainly rather than papered over: the originally reported both-commands-failed assertion was NEVER reproduced, across 148 runs (48 full-test executions = 240 concurrent pairs, plus 100 micro-iterations) at loads up to 98, above the 25-51 of the original gate failure. The supervisor-authorised scratch-build diagnostic (HUB_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT 5s -> 200ms, reverted) established it is not reachable via the readiness path: the hub still published a live record in time and the roles merely flipped. The fix does not depend on that interleaving — it removes an unsatisfiable wait for every waiter, so the unreproduced case is covered by construction rather than by guesswork.

TWO OF MY OWN DIAGNOSES WERE WRONG and are recorded as wrong in the task notes: (1) "the launcher's own child holds the lock and starves the peer" — false, the launcher execs the hub in the same pid and terminate_failed_launch kills it; (2) "HUB_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT being tighter than HUB_LIFECYCLE_TIMEOUT is the trigger" — false, disproved by the diagnostic. Both were corrected to the supervisor before any code was written on them.

Release note, Fixed: concurrent `cas hub start` / `cas hub restart` no longer stall ten seconds and report a spurious failure when another command has already brought up the hub you asked for.

task_title: Supervisor panes never wake for ordinary traffic: cas-dab2 gate denies every non-lifecycle row, so worker plans/merge requests/dispatch handoffs are delivered but invisible until the supervisor polls
close_reason:
Supervisor pane wakes are now decided from the sender CAS recorded at enqueue time, and a registered worker's merge request wakes an idle supervisor without a poll.

Delivered on factory/bold-heron-25 tip a3e81f6d, merged to epic/epic-v3-15-5-coordination-follow-ups-duplicate-mes-cas-55aa at c01ce1fa. Four commits: ee4d0dd2 (cherry-pick of true-panther-6's 7f178c0c — verified identical by patch-id, so that branch retires with nothing lost), 07f6361f, ffbc7080, fda51375. Each commit green and each leaves wakes functional; the schema/population half landed before the gate half deliberately, because NULL never wakes and a gate-first landing would have silently killed every wake CAS has today.

WHAT WAS WRONG
1. The reported bug: every non-lifecycle supervisor-addressed row was inbox-only, so the messages whose purpose is to unblock the supervisor waited for a poll (merge request 24346 parked a task in AwaitingMerge; dispatch handoff 24370 blocked a close; an execution plan sat unread while the supervisor sent a status check asking why no plan had arrived).
2. The cas-15f2 bypass, folded in by supervisor ruling 24559: the peer-supervisor allowance sat IN FRONT of cas-3dcb's envelope check and turned on names_a_registered_supervisor(agents, source) — a roster lookup of a caller-settable name. `cas factory message --from "<a real supervisor's name>"` therefore skipped envelope corroboration entirely and obtained a PTY write with arbitrary text. The old unit test modelled the forgery as "the roster said no" and could not see it.

WHAT LANDED
- prompt_queue.origin_agent_id / origin_kind: additive, nullable, written ONLY by CAS's own enqueue path from an already-authenticated caller. QueueOrigin {RegisteredAgent{agent_id}, Daemon, Unattributed}; the agent id is the registry id, not a display name, so role resolution cannot be spoofed by naming someone. No backfill — inventing provenance for rows whose sender was never recorded is the fiction the columns exist to prevent.
- Stamped: MCP coordination message/interrupt and factory clear_context -> RegisteredAgent, taken from the session's registry row and never from display_name, row_source, or get_agent_id()'s literal "unknown" fallback; 11 daemon relay sites -> Daemon. `cas factory message` and bridge POST /message cannot stamp AT ALL — they reach the store through methods that take no origin parameter, so there is no expression in those routes that can produce one. That is enforcement by type system, not a runtime default. Commander/hub is left unstamped deliberately: it has a real authenticated principal, but a device credential is not a registry id and minting one would be the same fiction.
- Gate re-keyed: supervisor_wake_class(sender, supervisor_name, source, prompt). Daemon + a lifecycle/worker-died/spawn/CI/attention envelope; Registered{Supervisor} + not this pane's own echo; Registered{Worker} + a CAS-attached <cas-merge-request>. Unstamped, Unattributed and Unresolvable never wake, whatever the payload says.
- message_status separates wake_not_applicable from wake_declined_by_policy with the reason. One prefix used to cover both a routine chat row and an eligible unblock request the pane refused — opposite facts, and the second hid in a wall of the first.
- Fail-safe: one Daemon-stamped <worker-attention kind="supervisor_unread"> per distinct backlog head, naming the unread count and the oldest sender, emitted from the delivery-stalled scan that previously bounced only to senders. This is how a blocker and a verification handoff reach an idle supervisor, satisfying the acceptance criteria's "or is surfaced by an equivalent unread mechanism" clause.
- Two doc comments corrected where they asserted a property that does not hold (factory_supervisor_overlap::names_a_registered_supervisor, and the gate's copy of the same claim). Both are now marked NOT AN AUTHENTICATION CHECK and retained as display/consistency only.

EVERY ACCEPTANCE CRITERION IS MET
- "A merge request … sent by a registered worker to its supervisor wakes the supervisor pane": met by the Registered{Worker} + <cas-merge-request> class.
- "verification handoff, or blocker … or is surfaced by an equivalent unread mechanism": met by the supervisor_unread backlog relay.
- "a message whose `source` string is caller-set and whose sender is not a registered agent still cannot obtain a PTY write": met, and enforced by the type system at the enqueue side as well as by the gate refusing Unstamped/Unattributed/Unresolvable.
- "message_status distinguishes 'wake not applicable' from 'wake declined by policy' with the reason": met by WakeOutcome, persisted as "wake_not_applicable: <reason>" / "wake_declined_by_policy: <reason>".
- "Duplicate delivery is either fixed or explained with the two writers named": explained and fixed. cas-cdf9 measured ONE writer performing two writes — delivery.rs:855 deliver_to_worker (the teams-inbox write, which Claude Code renders as <teammate-message>) and delivery.rs:876 pty_nudge (the same text typed into the pane, appearing as the bare "CAS provenance:" turn). director_events and surface_unseen_for_recipient are both exonerated by receipt evidence. Fixed at b3d834bb, already in this branch's base. I confirmed the two call sites exist as described; I did not re-derive the store measurements.

THE THREE JUDGEMENT CALLS, all ruled ACCEPTED AS DELIVERED by the supervisor (msg 24587)
1. `source` is still READ, but only for the Daemon class, where CAS wrote both the stamp and the source. Caught against an existing test: a Closed-transition lifecycle row carries a real envelope but no `lifecycle-wake:` prefix, so envelope-only would have started waking supervisors for progress FYIs — the exact cas-dab2 noise. It is authority nowhere.
2. Only the CAS-framed merge request wakes. Blockers and verification handoffs are free text, and waking on them means waking on a keyword — the check class this task removed. They are delivered through the unread-backlog relay above. The supervisor took the separate follow-up for CAS-emitted blocker/verification-dispatch envelopes as his own and instructed me not to open it; that is a future enhancement, not residual work from this task.
3. The peer-supervisor class trusts the stamped registry Supervisor role with no envelope requirement, stated out loud in the code rather than left implicit. There is no supervisor-to-supervisor envelope to corroborate against, and requiring one would kill the wake v3.15.4 just shipped.

Also load-bearing, and easy to misread as tidiness: wake-eligible rows are excluded from the unread count, because the summary is itself a lifecycle-wake row and would otherwise become its own backlog head without end. And `supervisor_unread` is registered in BOTH worker-attention parsers — the wake-corroboration check and message_ack's outbox-key bridge — since missing the second acks the durable notification and leaves the prompt relay visible in every later worker_status.

CLAIM DISCIPLINE, verbatim per ruling 24559: this raises the bar from "the caller must know a prefix and a tag grammar" to "the caller must be an authenticated registered agent".
